hotspots.text: The gilded knob crowning the roof at 38 meters, the apex of the triple eaves, carried on the Thunder God pillar where the vaulted dome converges.
hotspots.title: The gilded knob

hotspots.text: One of the four central Dragon Well pillars: 18.5 meters tall, 1.2 meters in diameter, read as the four seasons. They carry the heart of the dome.
hotspots.title: A Dragon Well pillar

hotspots.text: Interlocking wooden bracket sets, shrinking layer by layer to form the vaulted dome. The entire timber frame is joined with mortise and tenon: no nails anywhere in the building.
hotspots.title: Dougong brackets

hotspots.text: The lowest of the three eaves, covered in deep blue glazed tiles the color of the sky. All three tiers were blue only after the 1752 renovation; before that they mixed blue, yellow and green.
hotspots.title: The blue eaves

hotspots.text: The hall stands on a three-tiered circular marble terrace 6 meters high, each level ringed with carved white marble balustrades. Heaven is round: the whole composition is a circle on circles.
hotspots.title: The marble terrace

hotspots.text: Inside the roof, the dome converges toward the apex with no crossbeams: 28 pillars, bracket sets, rafters and lathes locked into one reinforced timber frame.
hotspots.title: The nail-less dome

intro: Every year the emperor came here to ask heaven for a good harvest, in a round wooden hall 38 meters high that holds together without a single nail. This is the most beautiful piece of carpentry ever put to a sacred purpose.
page_title: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body:
The Temple of Heaven was built in 1420 under the Ming Yongle Emperor, the same emperor who built the Forbidden City, as the place where the Son of Heaven worshipped heaven itself. The hall at its northern end began life as a rectangular building called the Great Sacrifice Hall, where heaven and earth were worshipped together.

In 1545 the Jiajing Emperor rebuilt it as the circular hall we see today and renamed it the Hall of Great Synthesis; in 1752 the Qianlong Emperor gave it its present name, the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. Every year in the first lunar month the emperor came here to perform the rites of praying for grain, asking for favorable weather and a bountiful harvest. In a country where agriculture was the foundation of the state, this was among the most important ceremonies in the imperial calendar. The hall burned down after a lightning strike in 1889 and was rebuilt in the years that followed, which is why the timber you see today is Qing dynasty work on a Ming idea.
sections.heading: The emperor's appointment with heaven

sections.body:
The hall is 38 meters high and about 30 to 36 meters across, and it is put together the hard way: completely in wood, without nails. Every joint is mortise and tenon, the bracket sets (dougong) shrinking layer by layer to carry the vaulted dome up to the gilded knob at the apex, which sits on the so-called Thunder God pillar.

The structure is a calendar in timber. Twenty-eight massive pillars carry the dome: four central Dragon Well pillars, 18.5 meters tall, for the four seasons; twelve inner gold pillars for the months of the year; twelve outer eave pillars for the twelve two-hour watches of the day. Other guides read all twenty-eight as the twenty-eight constellations. Either way the message is the same: the building is the cosmos, ordered and legible.

It stands on a three-tiered circular marble terrace 6 meters high, each level edged with carved white marble balustrades, and it is joined to the Imperial Vault of Heaven by the 360-meter Vermilion Steps Bridge. In 1998 the Temple of Heaven was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, described as a masterpiece illustrating a cosmogony of great importance to Chinese civilization.
sections.heading: Built without a single nail

sections.body:
The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests has a thinner filmography than its fame would suggest, and that is itself the story: it does not need movies. It is among the most photographed structures in China, the visual shorthand for Beijing in travel guides, documentaries and news coverage around the world. When a broadcast needs one image to say "China's capital," this blue triple roof on its white marble terraces is very often the one.

Its modern cultural moment came with the 2008 Beijing Olympics. In 2005 the Temple of Heaven underwent a 47-million-yuan restoration to prepare for the Games, completed in May 2006, and the hall stood at the center of the city's presentation of itself to the world: the ancient ritual architecture of the harvest prayers as the backdrop to a thoroughly modern Olympics. Between the ceremonies of emperors and the ceremonies of Olympiads, the building has spent six centuries as the place where China stages its relationship with heaven.

story_title: The story of the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests

timeline.text: The Yongle Emperor builds the Temple of Heaven; the hall begins as the rectangular Great Sacrifice Hall.
The Jiajing Emperor rebuilds the hall as a circular triple-eaved structure.
The Qianlong Emperor names it the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests; all three eaves become blue glazed tile.
Lightning burns the hall down; it is rebuilt in the years after.
The Temple of Heaven is inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A 47-million-yuan restoration prepares the temple for the 2008 Beijing Olympics.
